Locality Sensitivity Hashing

high-dimensional data.
• Locality sensitive hashing – this lecture
• Clustering

Many problems can be expressed as finding “similar” sets:

•
Find near-neighbors in high-dimensional space
Examples:

•
Pages with similar words
For duplicate detection, classification by topic

Customers who bought similar products
Users who watched similar movies

Images with similar features

Today’s lecture: Find pairs of similar docs
Main idea: Candidates
-- Pass 1: Take documents and hash them to buckets such that
documents that are similar hash to the same bucket
-- Pass 2: Only compare documents that are candidates
(i.e., they hashed to a same bucket)
Benefits: Instead of O(N2) comparisons, we need O(N)
comparisons to find similar documents

• In general, one throws items into buckets using several
different “hash functions”.
• You only examine those pairs of items that share a
bucket for at least one of these hashes

• Pros: Designed correctly, only a small fraction of pairs are
ever examined
• Cons: There are false negatives – pairs of similar items that
never even get considered

Consider the web as a database of many documents.  Want
to find pairs of documents with a lot of text in common.
• Mirror sites


2. Min-Hashing: Convert large sets to short signatures,
while preserving similarity.
3. Locality-Sensitive Hashing: Focus on pairs of signatures
most likely to be from similar documents (using a
threshold)

A different way: Shingles!

A 𝑘𝑘-shingle (or 𝑘𝑘-gram) for a document is a sequence of
𝑘𝑘tokens that appears in the doc
•
Tokens can be characters, words or something else,
depending on the application

•
Assume tokens = characters for examples in this
lecture

• Example:
𝒌𝒌= 𝟐𝟐; document 𝑫𝑫𝟏𝟏
= 𝒂𝒂𝒂𝒂𝒄𝒄𝒄𝒄𝒄𝒄
Set of 2-shingles: 𝑺𝑺(𝑫𝑫𝟏𝟏) = {𝒂𝒂𝒂𝒂, 𝒃𝒃𝒃𝒃, 𝒄𝒄𝒄𝒄}

• Properties of shingles:
• Documents that are similar will have many common
shingles.
Can detect similarity when small pieces of one document

appear in the other
• Ordering of characters are preserved
• Local effect: Changing a word only affects 𝒌𝒌-shingles
within distance 𝒌𝒌−𝟏𝟏from the word.

• Represent a document 𝑫𝑫𝟏𝟏by a set of its 𝒌𝒌-shingles 𝑪𝑪𝟏𝟏=
𝑺𝑺(𝑫𝑫𝟏𝟏)

•

Jaccard similarity

Encode sets using 0/1 Boolean
vectors:
• Rows = elements (shingles)
• Columns = sets (documents)

1 in row e and column s if and only if
e is a member of s

Column similarity is the Jaccard
similarity of the corresponding sets

Matrices are normally sparse
Example:
• sim(C1 ,C2) =3/6
• d(C1 ,C2) =1-3/6 = 3/6

• Sparse matrices are better represented by a list of
positions where a 1 appears


Recall triangular matrix vs triples method from last
lecture

•
We can keep the matrix picture in our minds to
understand the concepts

• In practice, it is common to compress long shingles (e.g.
9-shingles) into a 4 byte integer using a hash function
(e.g. MurmusHash3_32)


Uses the same amount of space as a 4-shingle
• Represent a document by the set of hash values of its
𝒌𝒌-shingles

• We may have hash collisions, but they are rare in practice,
and we will ignore them for the analysis in the rest of the
slides

• If 𝒌𝒌is too small, then most documents will have high
Jaccard similarity
• We should pick 𝒌𝒌to be large enough so that any shingle
will have low probability of appearing randomly in a
document

Example:
• If our documents are email, 𝑘𝑘= 5 is reasonable
• For large documents such as research papers, try 𝑘𝑘= 9

Clearly, the hash function depends on the similarity

• Not all similarity metrics have a suitable hash function.

For the Jaccard similarity, the similarity-preserving hash
function is called Min-Hashing.

strict.

approach 1.
